content: Rubella, also known as German measles, is a mild viral illness that primarily affects children and young adults. It typically manifests as a low-grade fever and a rash. However, when rubella infection occurs during pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester, it can lead to severe outcomes such as miscarriage, fetal death, stillbirth, or the birth of an infant with congenital malformations collectively referred to as congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Rubella virus is a leading cause of vaccine-preventable birth defects. The risk of congenital infection and associated defects is highest during the first 12 weeks of gestation and decreases thereafter. Defects are rare if the infection occurs after the 20th week of gestation. Common congenital defects caused by CRS include cataracts, congenital heart disease, hearing impairment, and developmental delays. Infants with CRS often present with multiple defects, although some may exhibit only a single defect, most commonly hearing impairment. Globally, the number of reported CRS cases increased from 302 in 2012 to 603 in 2020. This rise is attributed to the initiation of CRS surveillance and reporting in several populous countries, including Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, and Pakistan, as well as changes in reporting practices in Pakistan in 2020. In the South-East Asia Region, the number of countries reporting CRS cases increased from two in 2002 to ten in 2016. Countries such as North Korea, Sri Lanka, and Thailand include CRS case reporting as part of their national integrated disease surveillance programs. The South-East Asia Region bears the highest burden of CRS cases globally. Infants with CRS or congenital rubella infection (CRI) can shed live rubella virus for extended periods, with approximately 60% shedding the virus during the first four months of life. These infants are highly infectious and should be considered contagious until two clinical specimens, obtained at least one month apart after the age of three months, test negative for rubella virus detection or isolation. Until this time, infection control measures must be strictly followed. In hospital settings, these infants should remain in isolation, and caregivers must adhere to universal precautions. Close contacts, including family members and friends involved in the care of such infants, should either be immune or vaccinated against rubella as per national policy. In areas where follow-up testing of confirmed CRS and CRI cases is not feasible, emphasis must be placed on ensuring that close contacts and healthcare workers are vaccinated against rubella. In healthcare settings, contact precautions should be implemented for every detected CRS and CRI case. Pregnant women should not be exposed to infants with CRS or CRI; if exposure occurs, they should be tested for rubella. Active community searches should be conducted to identify additional CRS cases and to review the vaccination status of children in the locality. All unimmunized children or those without available immunization records should be vaccinated with a measlesand rubella-containing vaccine according to national recommendations. Contact tracing is recommended among mothers of infants with CRS or CRI to identify the source of the rubella virus in the mother. Rubella IgM antibodies may persist for up to one year following vaccination, but approximately 50% of CRS cases are IgM-negative by six months of age, depending on the sensitivity of the test. Infants suspected of having CRS who test negative for IgM shortly after birth should be retested at one month of age or shortly thereafter. Laboratory confirmation of CRS in infants older than six months should not rely solely on IgM testing if the result is negative. In such cases, serial IgG testing should be conducted at least one month apart to determine if IgG antibody levels are sustained over several months. Virus isolation techniques should also be employed to test whether infants with congenital rubella are shedding the virus. Congenitally infected infants may shed and transmit rubella virus for up to one year, potentially serving as a source of rubella outbreaks. Therefore, it is crucial to continue testing for the virus throughout the first year of life to ensure that infection control measures remain in place until virus shedding ceases. Viral shedding can be confirmed to have ceased by obtaining two negative viral test results from specimens collected one month apart from infants at least three months of age. Genotyping of the rubella virus can provide information about the source of the virus. In endemic settings, genotype testing should be conducted at least once for every chain of rubella transmission. Currently, there is no specific treatment available for CRS beyond the clinical management of associated congenital abnormalities. Patients should be cared for and followed up by experienced personnel in accordance with national treatment guidelines. The number of CRS cases generally increases six to eight months after a rubella outbreak. An increase in CRS cases may indicate wider circulation of the rubella virus in the population, suggesting the occurrence of a past or ongoing rubella outbreak. CRS surveillance should be established or strengthened in maternity hospitals, pediatric hospitals, neonatal intensive care units, and among specialists treating infants with cardiac, hearing, or eye deficits. Hospitals in outbreak areas should serve as sentinel sites if they are not already designated as such. Passive CRS surveillance systems should be enhanced with active case-finding in facilities located in outbreak-affected areas to identify infants with CRS or CRI who may be prolonging the outbreak by shedding live rubella virus. CRS surveillance should continue for at least nine months after the last rubella case. If not already in place, a pregnancy registry should be established to document the pregnancy outcomes of infected and exposed women. Outcomes include miscarriages, fetal deaths, CRS cases, infants with CRI, and unaffected infants. Infants with CRS or CRI should be considered infectious until two clinical specimens, obtained one month apart, test negative for rubella virus detection or isolation. Infection control procedures should be followed until this time. In hospitals, these infants should remain in isolation, and caregivers should adhere to universal precautions. Close contacts, family members, and friends involved in the care or handling of such infants should either be immune or vaccinated against rubella, as per national policy. In areas where follow-up testing of confirmed CRS and CRI cases is not feasible, emphasis must be placed on ensuring that close contacts and healthcare workers are vaccinated for rubella. In healthcare settings, contact precautions should be implemented for every detected CRS and CRI case. Pregnant women should not be exposed to infants with CRS or CRI; if exposed, they should be tested for rubella. A retrospective review of medical records in health institutions can be conducted annually to monitor the sensitivity of the CRS surveillance system. For countries unable to establish or maintain CRS surveillance, a retrospective review can help identify CRS cases. Such reviews can aid in estimating the disease burden or provide baseline data to measure the impact of vaccine introduction. However, a limitation of this approach is that retrospectively identified cases often lack laboratory confirmation and, therefore, a definitive diagnosis. Serological assessments of rubella IgG antibody levels among women of reproductive age, conducted in a survey setting, may help evaluate population immunity against rubella and protection against CRS in newborns. Rubella IgG can be acquired through both vaccination and natural infection; therefore, serosurveys are not purely a reflection of vaccination coverage. A serological survey is not a substitute for CRS surveillance but can complement it. CRS cases should be reported separately from clinical rubella cases. The doctor should transmit the case notification form or core information to public health personnel. Once the case investigation is completed, the case-based data should be transferred from the local level to higher administrative levels in the surveillance system (state or national level). Each suspected case should be assigned a unique case identification number.
